items.text: Sales since {period_start} are {sales_ptd} against {sales_ptd_ly} on the same days last year ({yoy_ptd}); each week was ahead of the same week last year ({weeks_ahead} of {weeks_total}).

First-time Gen Z customers rose from {genz_new_customers_ly} to {genz_new_customers}. Sales from them are {genz_new_diff} vs last year, {genz_new_share} of total growth; {genz_new_store_share} of that change was in stores.
Returning Gen Z customers fell from {genz_repeat_customers_ly} to {genz_repeat_customers}, and sales from them are {genz_repeat_sales_yoy} vs last year ({genz_repeat_diff}).

{top1_name} ({top1_diff}) and {top2_name} ({top2_diff}) had the largest product gains; women's apparel is {apparel_yoy} vs last year, and {overstock_names} each have more than {overstock_threshold} weeks of stock.
This week so far is {wow} vs the same days last week and {wtd_yoy} vs the same days last year.
Week {last_week_no} was {last_week_yoy} vs last year, against {prior_week_yoy} the week before.
First-time Gen Z customers this week so far: {genz_new_wtd}, against {genz_new_last_week} on the same days last week.

Weeks of stock left fell from {top1_cover_prev} to {top1_cover} for {top1_name} and from {top2_cover_prev} to {top2_cover} for {top2_name}; families that changed stock status since last week: {status_changes}.
The two largest product gains have the fewest weeks of stock left: {top1_name} {top1_cover} against {top1_cover_ly} last year, {top2_name} {top2_cover} against {top2_cover_ly}.
{genz_family1_name} and {genz_family2_name} are also the top two families by sales to first-time Gen Z customers ({genz_family1_diff} and {genz_family2_diff}).
The share of first-time Gen Z customers in Insider fell from {genz_new_insider_ly} to {genz_new_insider}; among returning customers it is {repeat_insider}.
Most customers appear once in this extract, so returning customers are identified by their customer status, not by a measured repeat rate.
